analysis.text:
Gamini Perera was allotted Lot A depicted in Partition Plan No. 2525 dated 2 February 1981, made by S. Silva, Licensed Surveyor, bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama, containing in extent 10 perches, by a final decree of a partition case bearing No. 111/P dated 2 February 1985 entered in the District Court of Homagama.

Gamini Perera, by Deed of Gift No. 515 dated 10 March 1986, attested by R. Liyanage, Notary Public, gifted the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 absolutely and irrevocably to his son, Suresh Perera, subject to the life interest of Gamini Perera and his wife Vinitha. Gamini Perera died on 12 June 1990 due to heart failure. Vinitha revoked her life interest over the said Lot A depicted in Plan No. 2525 by Deed of Revocation of Life Interest No. 525 dated 25 February 1991, attested by S. Sapumal, Notary Public.

Suresh Perera married Kanthi and had two children, namely Rakitha and Muditha. Muditha died due to an accident on 5 June 2023, unmarried and issueless. Rakitha married Ann and died on 2 July 2022.

Suresh Perera died on 10 December 1995 intestate. Suresh Perera had an offspring named Samantha from his first marriage, who is a citizen of the United States of America.

1. Draw up the pedigree showing the devolution of title from Gamini Perera up to the present owners in relation to the land and premises bearing Assessment No. 20, Flower Road, Homagama. **(15 marks)**
2. What are the shares presently owned by each heir in the property? **(4 marks)**
3. Can Samantha become entitled to the intestate estate of Suresh Perera? Discuss with reference to the provisions of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014, as amended by the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) (Amendment) Act No. 21 of 2018. **(2 marks)**
4. Explain the rules set out in sections 22 to 26 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876. **(4 marks)**

**Total: 25 marks**

claims.text: Under Section 2(1) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014, transfer of title of land in Sri Lanka to a foreigner is prohibited unless exempted under section 3. However, whether Samantha can inherit the estate cannot be fully discussed because section 3, definitions of 'transfer' and 'foreigner', and the text of the 2018 amendment to section 5A are missing.

Under Section 22 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876, when a person dies intestate leaving a surviving spouse, that spouse inherits one-half of the deceased's property. Section 22 also states that nothing in the Ordinance relieves a husband from liability to maintain her children. The rules in sections 23 to 26 are missing from the provided text.

3. Somar’s employer requests him to act under section 31 of the Notaries Ordinance when attesting the deed without a full title search. Is this permitted? Explain. **(2 marks)**

claims.text: Under the Notaries Ordinance, a notary can execute a deed without checking the title at the Land Registry if the parties to the transaction authorize the notary in writing to dispense with the search.
Dispensing with the title search is only permitted if the 'parties to the transaction' authorize the notary in writing.

Consequently, an instruction from Somar's employer does not permit him to dispense with the search under the Ordinance, unless the employer is also a party to the transaction and authorizes it in writing.
The provided statutory sections and amendments do not contain any rules or procedures regarding transactions in which a notary or their relative has an interest.

analysis.text:
> **Note:** This page was blurred. The wording below is reconstructed from the visible text.

A Notary who has practised in Homagama since approximately 1987 intends to apply for appointment/registration under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998 and other relevant written law.

1. How do the requirements under the relevant law apply to the Commissioner of Title Settlement and to what types of land would title be registered? **(4 marks)**
2. Could both the owner and occupier make an application in respect of the land? Can the application be rejected without an inquiry? **(4 marks)**
3. A deed affecting land is executed, but the instrument is not presented for registration within the prescribed period. Is registration mandatory, and what is the legal consequence of non-registration? **(4 marks)**
4. Who may present an instrument for registration according to the Registration of Title Act/Registration of Documents Ordinance? **(3 marks)**

**Total: 15 marks**

claims.text: Upon receiving certified copies of cadastral maps, the Commissioner of Title Settlement is required to publish a Notice in the Gazette, calling for claimants to the specified land parcel to submit their claims within a prescribed period from the date of publication. The provided sections do not specify the types of land to which title would be registered.

The retrieved sections do not state whether both an owner and occupier can make an application or if it can be rejected without inquiry. However, Section 24 of the Registration of Title Act provides that a District Court may make orders, such as a Declaration of Title or order for sale, only after due inquiry following a reference under section 21 or an appeal under section 22.

Under Section 7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, registration is not mandatory for basic validity, but an unregistered instrument executed on or after January 1, 1864 is void against parties claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument.

Section 7(4) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance states that registration of an instrument does not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any validity or effect other than the priority conferred by section 7.

The Registration of Documents Ordinance indicates that an instrument is presented by a person or his agent, as the Registrar must endorse the instrument and return it on demand to the person who presented it or his agent.

(2) But fraud or collusion in obtaining such subsequent instrument or in securing the prior registration thereof shall defeat the priority of the person claiming thereunder. claims.text: The provided text does not contain a general provision specifying all persons authorized to present standard instruments for registration. However, under the base Ordinance, it indicates that a person presenting an instrument must be authorized by the Ordinance to present it (SRC005:s36(1)(a)), and specifically, a judgment creditor may present a seizure priority notice (SRC005:s31(1)). Under the 2022 Amendment Act, a caveator who has or claims to have a right, title, or interest to a land may present a caveat (SRC009:s32(1)(a)). Additionally, an instrument can be returned after registration to the person who presented it or their agent (SRC005:s28(1)).

Under the Ordinance, the Registrar may, at their discretion, refuse to register an instrument if: (a) they suspect the person presenting it is not authorized, until authorization is proved (SRC005:s36(1)(a)); or (b) the instrument does not comply with the Ordinance or other written laws regarding its form or execution (SRC005:s36(1)(b)). Additionally, the Registrar must (mandatorily) refuse registration if: (a) the instrument is liable to stamp duty but not duly stamped (SRC005:s36(2)(a)); or (b) the required registration fee has not been paid (SRC005:s36(2)(b)).

If an error or omission in registration is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General, they must issue a written notice in the prescribed form to the parties (for deeds), executor or administrator (for wills), or presenter (for other instruments) (SRC005:s35(1)). If an interested person proves that notice cannot be issued due to death, legal incapacity, or other sufficient cause, the Registrar-General may make the correction order without notice (SRC005:s35(1) Proviso). The Registrar-General then orders the correction, which is executed by the concerned Registrar, but this correction does not affect priority accrued beforehand (SRC005:s35(1)). If the error and correction are in different folios, they must be cross-referenced (SRC005:s35(2)). An aggrieved party can challenge a refusal to correct by suing in the District Court within 30 days (SRC005:s35(3)).

claims.text: Under the Apartment Ownership (Special Provisions) Act, No. 23 of 2018, for certain Condominium Properties owned by designated state agencies and constructed before December 31, 2009, the owner must submit to the Registrar at the time of registration a written declaration obtained from the Director-General of the Department of Buildings certifying the safety of occupation of the Condominium Property. General provisions defining a Condominium Declaration are missing from the provided text.

The provided statutes refer to a 'Condominium Plan', 'Plan of redivision', and 'Plan of amalgamation' and outline procedures for their registration or amendment, but they do not list the specific types of Condominium Plans or define the differences among them.

The heading of Section 24 of the Apartment Ownership Law references 'Provisions of Partition Act not to apply in certain cases', but the substantive statutory text setting out the details and explanation of this exclusion is omitted and missing from the provided source.

By a Final Decree dated 5 May 2018, entered in partition case bearing No. 3535/P of the District Court of Nugegoda, Ajith Silva was allotted all that allotment of land marked Lot 2 depicted in Plan No. 1616 dated 2 March 2010, made by A. C. Perera, Licensed Surveyor, of the land called Kahatagahawatte, bearing Assessment No. 12, Temple Road, Nugegoda, containing in extent 15 perches.

Ajith Silva, by Deed of Gift No. 515 dated 10 December 2018, attested by P. C. Nonis, Notary Public, gifted the said Lot 2 depicted in Plan No. 1616 to Prabash Silva, the elder son of Ajith, subject to the life interest of the donor, and subject to the condition that Prabash shall not sell, mortgage or otherwise deal with the land, but may enjoy the produce thereof during his lifetime. On the death of Prabash, the property shall devolve free of all conditions to Subash, the younger son of Ajith Silva.

Ajith had three children, namely Prabash, Subash and Shehani, by his second marriage to Yamuna. Ajith had another daughter named Kushani from his first marriage to Sumana.

Ajith Silva died intestate on 2 March 2019, and Prabash Silva died intestate on 2 June 2019.

Prabash had two daughters, namely Sunali and Bimali, by his first wife Sheela, and two sons, namely Brian and Rian, by his second wife Linda. Sheela died intestate on 5 August 2019. Brian married Sara and thereafter died in an accident on 25 September 2021 without having children. Sunali died on 10 October 2023 unmarried and issueless.

1. Draw up the pedigree showing the devolution of title from Ajith Silva up to the present owners in relation to the property bearing Assessment No. 12, Temple Road, Nugegoda. **(20 marks)**
2. What are the shares presently owned by each heir in the property? **(5 marks)**

**Total: 25 marks**

claims.text: The provided statutes do not contain a lawyer-verified deed template or drafting-model source to draft the operative clause of a Deed of Gift. However, under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, any deed or instrument affecting immovable property must be in writing, signed by every executant, and attested by a licensed notary public and witnesses.

Under the Stamp Duty Act and the Western Province Financial Statute, stamp duty on an instrument of gift is calculated on the value of the property conveyed. If the property is gifted subject to a reservation in favour of the donor or another person, the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property as if it had been gifted without that reservation. The supplied text does not outline the historical rules or distinction for calculating value before and after 31 March 1977.

Under both the Western Province Financial Statute and the Stamp Duty Act, the stamp duty for Mark Perera's gift of land subject to a life interest reservation must be calculated on the value of the property as if it had been gifted without that reservation. However, the exact stamp duty payable cannot be calculated because the applicable stamp duty rates or schedules are not provided in the text.

hits.excerpt: 48. (1) Where any property is conveyed by an instrument, the stamp duty with which such instrument is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property conveyed. (2) Where any property transferred for a consideration is subject to any mortgage, encumbrances or reservation of interest, stamp duty with which the instrument of transfer is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property transferred, without any deduction for the mortgage, encumbrances or reservation. (3) Where any property is gifted subject to any reservation in favour of the donor or any other person, stamp duty with which the instrument of gift is chargeable shall be calculated on the value of the property gifted as if that property had been gifted to the donee without that reservation.
